faqs.q: Iguanas are damaging my Fort Myers seawall — what is the real fix?
faqs.a: Removal plus burrow denial. Green iguanas dig burrows into seawall banks that can undermine the structure, so we remove the animals working your waterfront — lawful here, as iguanas are a Chapter 68-5 Prohibited species FWC encourages landowners to have removed — and then collapse and fill burrow systems and trim the basking-and-feeding vegetation that draws replacements. They can never be relocated, so the population answer is consistent removal at your property plus habitat change, which together drop sightings sharply within a season.

Fort Myers.wildlife_intro:
Fort Myers spreads from the Edison-era downtown and McGregor Boulevard's royal palms to the Caloosahatchee waterfront, Cape Coral's bridge neighbor, and suburbs reaching toward Lehigh. Burrowing owls hold protected lots in the city's open areas, iguanas graze the riverfront and canal banks — Fort Myers is deep-south, established-colony territory — roof rats feast in the royal palms, and raccoons den from Dean Park's historic homes to the newest south-side subdivisions.

McGregor's palms are a rat superhighway, and Fort Myers inspections trace palm-to-roof contact with unusual care. Iguana removal is a standing service here, done humbly and legally: removal on your property, never relocation, plus burrow and vegetation management along seawalls. Owl burrows on vacant lots are flagged and referred. Bats in the historic district's buildings follow the state season, and our quotes say so plainly.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Cape Coral?

faqs.q: We are buying a Cape Coral lot with owl burrows — what does that mean?
faqs.a: It means your lot has a protected tenant and a permitting step. Burrowing owls are State Threatened; their burrows cannot be destroyed without an FWC permit, and building plans route around that process, which your builder and the city's environmental staff know well — Cape Coral manages more owl lots than anywhere. Our role is early identification: confirming burrows before purchase or design money is spent, so the permit path is a schedule item, not a surprise. It is not, at any point, a removal service.

Lehigh Acres.wildlife_intro:
Lehigh Acres is Lee County's vast inland grid — a quarter-million platted lots, half of them still empty, canals throughout, and a working-class community spread over 96 square miles of former ranchland. Vacant-lot habitat drives everything: raccoons, armadillos, tortoises, and snakes use the empty grid, roof rats and squirrels use the houses, and the canals hold herons, otters, and the occasional gator. Growth keeps converting lots, which keeps displacing animals into the built streets.

Lehigh service is priced for Lehigh — big-grid math, inspections that account for the vacant lots on both sides, and exclusion hardened for constant pressure. Tortoise burrows on owned lots are identified and buffered; on build lots, we tell buyers to start the FWC permit conversation early. Attic work is the standard craft done thoroughly, because in a grid this empty, a soft-sealed house is the neighborhood's den of choice.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Bonita Springs?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the home needs afterward. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: What is digging the small sand mounds in my Bonita Springs yard?
faqs.a: That depends on the shape. Eastern moles leave raised surface tunnels and small molehills, armadillos leave scattered digging in beds and lawn edges, and in sandy north and central Florida soils a southeastern pocket gopher leaves a row of sand mounds. A large burrow with a wide, half-moon apron of sand is different — that is likely a gopher tortoise burrow, which is protected, carries a 25-foot permit buffer, and must be left alone. Call us and describe the digging and we will identify it before any work is planned.

Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — canal city of Cape Coral, coastal suburbs, barrier islands, and inland Lehigh Acres — and features such as Caloosahatchee River, Sanibel Island, Estero Bay, Six Mile Cypress Slough keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Bonita Springs jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Sanibel?
faqs.a: Sanibel quotes reflect island logistics and Gulf-grade materials, stated plainly in writing after inspection — the number is the work and the ferry-free causeway reality, nothing hidden. Structure-only scope keeps protected species entirely out of the figure, as they should be.

faqs.q: An alligator lives in our Sanibel neighborhood pond — what is the protocol?
faqs.a: Follow the city's: Sanibel residents live under a well-known alligator coexistence policy — observe from at least 60 feet by city guidance, never feed (illegal statewide and the root of nearly every problem), keep pets leashed and out of the water, and report an alligator that is four feet or more and threatening, or any animal that has lost its fear of people, to the police non-emergency line or FWC's nuisance alligator program, which alone sends trappers. A pond gator sunning across the water is a resident, not an emergency, and island life is built around knowing the difference.

Sanibel.wildlife_intro:

Wildlife is not a problem category here so much as the population: alligators in the freshwater wetlands, raccoons, marsh rabbits, bobcats, and an official city alligator protocol residents actually read. Removal work exists — rats and raccoons in the island's homes — but it is practiced inside the strictest coexistence culture in Florida.

Sanibel service is discreet and rule-forward. Alligators follow the city's protocol and FWC's program, full stop; we handle the structure animals — roof rats in island attics, raccoons in chimneys — with exclusion materials rated for the Gulf environment and a light footprint. Post-storm rebuilding left many homes with new rooflines and the same old gaps; our island inspections audit those transitions. Protected everything else gets a referral and a respectful distance.

faqs.a: At rough-in, before insulation and drywall. Fort Myers Beach occupies Estero Island — seven miles of Gulf frontage, a Times Square pier district, bay-side canals on Matanzas Pass, and a town still visibly rebuilding after Hurricane Ian. Rebuilding defines the wildlife picture: new construction beside storm-damaged shells, displaced raccoons and rats colonizing whatever stands, and vacant structures that become animal housing within a season. Our beach work is rebuild-aware: inspections of repaired homes concentrate on the seams between old and new — where roof meets addition is where the rats enter — and vacant or damaged structures get humane clearing assessments before demolition or renovation. For everyone rebuilding, one piece of timing advice: seal the new roofline completely before interior finishes go in, because exclusion after the fact costs triple.
